transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, it’s a bit of a story, I suppose. My wife actually is the one who pushed me to make the appointment. We’ve been married for over thirty years, and since I stopped working a little while back, we obviously spend a lot more time together around the house. And lately, there’s been a lot going on with my family. My cousin has been needing some help getting around, so there’s a lot of coordination happening with his schedule. Appointments, rides, who is picking him up, that sort of thing. 

Anyway, what really brought me in today is that my wife will be sitting right there in the kitchen or the living room, telling me all about my cousin’s appointments or who is giving him rides for the week, and I am looking right at her. I mean, I’m making eye contact, I’m nodding, I really think I am paying attention to her. But then, literally a minute later, I realize I didn’t actually take in half of what she just said. It’s like the words just went in one ear and out the other, even though I was staring right at her face. 

It’s incredibly frustrating for her, because she thinks I’m just ignoring her on purpose, which I’m absolutely not doing. I want to help out with my cousin, I really do. But I just... I don't know, my mind must just drift off even when I'm looking right at someone. So she finally told me I needed to come talk to a professional about it, and well, here I am.
Have you noticed any other changes in your thinking or memory lately, such as forgetting things more often, getting lost in familiar places, or having trouble following conversations?

Well, I wouldn't say I'm getting lost in familiar places or anything like that. I know my way around town just fine, thank goodness. But, you know, now that you mention forgetting things... yes, absolutely, I have noticed that. It's been happening more and more lately, and it's honestly driving me a bit up the wall. 

For example, just the other day, I meant to return a call from the doctor's office—my own doctor, not my cousin's, though I do have to keep track of his too, which just adds to the confusion. Anyway, I got the voicemail, thought to myself, "Okay, I'll call them back right after I finish my coffee." And then... poof. Completely gone from my mind until the next morning when I saw the little notification on my phone again. 

And it's not just phone calls. I'll be meaning to pick up a prescription at the pharmacy. I'll even write it down on a little sticky note, put the sticky note on the counter right where I can see it, and I'll still walk right out the door without it, and then I'm halfway down the street before I realize I completely forgot to stop by the pharmacy. Or, and this is the one that really gets my wife upset, I'll be trying to leave the house on time for one of my cousin's appointments. I know what time we have to be there, I know how long it takes to drive there, but somehow, I'll start doing something else—maybe I'll decide to check the mail, or I'll notice a lightbulb is out in the hallway and think I should change it real quick—and suddenly we're running ten minutes late and I'm rushing out the door. It's just these everyday things I mean to do, and they just slip right through the cracks.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or losing interest in activities you used to enjoy?

No, no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling sad or down in the dumps or anything like that. I mean, sure, it's a bit frustrating when I forget things or my wife gets annoyed with me, but I'm not depressed. I actually still really enjoy my hobbies. I've always been a bit of a tinkerer, you know? I have this workbench out in the garage, and I love going out there and just messing around with old radios or small engines. I've been working on this one vintage lawnmower for... well, it feels like ages now. I keep finding new parts it needs, or I'll get it all taken apart and then realize I don't have the right wrench for a specific bolt, so then I have to go to the hardware store. And you know how it is at the hardware store, you go in for one wrench and you come out with a whole new set of drill bits and some weather stripping you remembered you needed for the back door. 

But anyway, to answer your question, I still love doing all that. I'll spend hours out there if my wife doesn't come out to tell me it's time for dinner. And I still enjoy watching the baseball games on TV, and we have a couple of friends we get together with for cards on Friday nights. We play Euchre, usually, sometimes Hearts if another couple can't make it. So, no, my mood is generally pretty good, I think. It's really just this... this scatterbrained feeling that's the problem, not feeling sad.
Have you ever seen, heard, or felt things that others don’t seem to notice, or have you had thoughts that others find unusual or hard to understand?

Oh, heavens no. Nothing like that. I mean, I know sometimes I get a little distracted or I might lose my train of thought, but I'm definitely not seeing things that aren't there or hearing voices or anything of that nature. My mind just wanders, it doesn't play tricks on me like that. 

I actually had a neighbor once, years ago, back when we lived in our old house on Elm Street—nice house, big oak tree in the front yard, though the roots played absolute havoc with the plumbing, let me tell you. Anyway, this neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he started getting up there in years and he would swear he saw people walking through his backyard at all hours of the night. He even called the police a few times, and they'd come out with their flashlights and search the bushes, but there was never anyone there. It turned out it was his medication or something, or maybe just his eyes going bad, I don't really know for sure. But it was quite a to-do for the neighborhood for a few months. 

But no, I've never experienced anything like that myself. I see what everyone else sees, I hear what everyone else hears—well, when I'm actually paying attention, that is! And as for unusual thoughts, I think I'm pretty grounded. I just think about normal things, you know, my projects in the garage, the baseball scores, what we're having for dinner, how my cousin is doing. Just regular, everyday stuff. Nothing out of the ordinary or hard for anyone to understand, except maybe why I can't seem to remember to pick up the dry cleaning when I drive right past the place! But no, no strange visions or unusual thoughts whatsoever.
Have you been having trouble organizing tasks or keeping track of multiple things at once?

Well, organizing tasks... no, I wouldn't say I have trouble with that. I haven't really noticed any issues keeping track of multiple things, to be honest. Actually, I've always prided myself on being quite organized. Take my filing system at home, for instance. Since I'm not working anymore, I handle all the household paperwork and all of my cousin's medical bills, which, let me tell you, is a full-time job in itself. But I have this whole system set up in the spare room—it used to be my son's room before he moved out to Denver, well, technically Aurora, but everyone just says Denver. Anyway, I bought this heavy-duty, four-drawer metal filing cabinet from a garage sale a few years back. Took me and my neighbor two hours just to get it up the front steps, scratched the doorframe a bit, but we got it in. 

But I use color-coded folders for everything in there. Blue is for utilities, red is for medical—I even separate my medical from my cousin's medical by using different colored tabs, you know, the little plastic ones that you slide the paper label into? Though sometimes the paper slips out and you have to fish it out of the bottom of the drawer, which is a bit of a nuisance. And for my daily tasks, I have this big magnetic whiteboard calendar right on the front of the refrigerator. The bank gives them out every January, the main branch downtown, not the smaller one by the grocery store. I write everything down on there with dry-erase markers. 

I'll have the lawnmower project going, the grocery list, the cousin's transport schedule, paying the property taxes, all going at once, and I keep track of the big picture just fine. I mean, sure, like I said earlier, I might walk out the door and forget the specific sticky note I just wrote, or get sidetracked by a burnt-out lightbulb when I'm supposed to be leaving, but the actual organizing of the tasks? The planning out of multiple things and knowing what's on my plate? No, I've got a pretty good handle on that. I know exactly what needs to be done and how my systems are arranged. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm having trouble organizing or keeping track of things at all.
Have you been having trouble starting tasks on your own or finishing things once you’ve started them?

Starting them? No, no, I don't think I have much trouble getting started. Like I said, I've got my whiteboard and my systems, so I'm usually pretty good about jumping right into whatever needs doing. But... finishing them. Now that, well, that might be a slightly different story. It’s not that I completely abandon a whole project, not usually anyway, but I’ll begin something really simple, just a standard everyday chore, and then I'll notice later that I left one or two steps completely unfinished. 

Take my cousin’s pill organizer, for example. I do that every Sunday morning right after we have our coffee. He’s got one of those big plastic ones with the morning, noon, and night compartments, you know the kind? It’s got the little raised bumps for braille on it even though he’s not blind, he just has some mild cataracts, but anyway, I’ll get all the prescription bottles out—and he takes a lot of them, blood pressure, cholesterol, a water pill, you name it—and I’ll be popping them into the little slots, going right down the days of the week. And I'll get just about done, maybe I'm on the Saturday evening slot, and I'll think I'm finished, or maybe I'll turn around to throw away an empty cotton ball from a new bottle, and then three hours later I'll walk back into the kitchen for a glass of water and realize I left the Sunday lids popped wide open and two of the bottles sitting right there on the counter without their caps screwed back on. 

Or, you know, it happens when I'm cooking, too. I do a lot of the cooking since I'm home, mostly grilling in the summer but this time of year I do a lot of stews and roasts. I’ll be cleaning the prep table after I'm done chopping the onions and carrots and celery—a mirepoix, they call it on those cooking shows—and I'll wipe down the surface, wash the cutting board, dry the chef's knife. I always hand wash the good knives, by the way, you should never put those in the dishwasher because the heat ruins the temper of the steel and dulls the blade. But anyway, I'll do all that, and then I'll walk away and completely forget to wipe up the little pile of onion skins I swept into the corner of the counter, or I'll just leave the bottle of antibacterial spray sitting right in the middle of the table instead of putting it back under the sink where it belongs. My wife will come in and sigh and put the spray away herself. It's just... I get ninety-five percent of the way there, and then it's like my brain just checks out and moves on before I actually do that final step.
Do you find yourself getting easily distracted or having trouble staying focused on tasks once you've started them?

Well, staying focused... yes, I suppose that is something that happens to me. Especially if it's something that takes a bit of time or requires me to sit still for a while. For instance, since I'm not working, I do quite a bit of volunteer work for our church—St. Jude's, over on 4th Street. It's a lovely parish, beautiful stained glass, though the parking lot is an absolute nightmare on Sunday mornings because the painted lines are entirely faded and people just park wherever they please. 

Anyway, I help out with the parish planning committee, and I handle a lot of the food logistics for our events. So, if I sit down at my desk to work out a catering order for, say, the annual pancake breakfast or the Lenten fish fry, or if I have to listen through a parish planning call—we do a lot of them over the computer or on conference lines now, which is a whole other headache because half the committee forgets how to unmute themselves—I always start off fine. I really do. I'm sitting there, I've got my notepad out, my pen in hand, and I'm totally dialed in. 

But before long, I don't even realize it's happening, my mind just completely wanders. I'll be staring right at the spreadsheet, or the person on the phone will be halfway through a budget report, and I'll suddenly snap back and realize I haven't absorbed a single thing for the last ten minutes. I'll actually have to go back over the exact same notes I just took, or the menu I was just looking at, and read them all over again like I never even read them in the first place. It’s like my eyes are moving over the paper, but my brain has just packed up and gone on a little vacation without telling me. So yes, once I'm in the middle of something like that, holding onto that focus can be remarkably difficult.
How long have you been experiencing these difficulties with your attention and forgetfulness? Have they been getting worse over time, or have they stayed about the same?

Well, let me think about that. How long... you know, I've always had my little quirks, maybe a bit of a wandering mind here and there, but as far as it being a real difficulty? Something that actually feels like a hurdle? I'd have to say it's been noticeably harder for about, oh, let's see, it must be right around eleven months now. Yes, eleven months almost exactly. 

Because that’s right when my cousin moved in with us. He had to have surgery—a full hip replacement, actually, on the right side. The surgeon told us the joint was just completely bone on bone, which sounds absolutely excruciating, doesn't it? They used one of those titanium and ceramic joints, supposed to last twenty years. Anyway, his own house is one of those split-levels built back in the late seventies, with the steep stairs right when you walk in the front door, so there was just no way on earth he could manage his recovery there. 

So, my wife and I, we took him in. We set him up in our den on the first floor because it has the good pull-out sofa and it's right next to the half-bath, which makes things easier for a man on a walker. But ever since he got here, and I took on managing all his pills—like I was telling you about earlier with the Sunday organizer—and his appointments and his physical therapy schedule... well, that's when things really took a turn. It’s definitely gotten worse since then. Having that extra layer of responsibility in the house, it's like it pushed my brain just past its limit, and that's when the forgetfulness and the trouble focusing really started standing out to me. So, yes, about eleven months, and it’s definitely felt worse over that time.
Have you had days where you don’t feel like doing anything, even things you usually enjoy, like working on your projects or watching baseball?

Days where I don't want to do anything? Oh, no, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Not at all. If there's a baseball game on, you can bet I'm right there in my recliner. I've been a huge fan of the game since I was a little boy. You know, they changed the rules recently with that new pitch clock, which I have to admit I have very mixed feelings about. On the one hand, I suppose it speeds up the game so you aren't sitting there for four hours, but on the other hand, the tension between pitches, the batter stepping out to adjust his batting gloves, the pitcher staring him down—that was all part of the psychological warfare of the sport! It's a thinking man's game. But anyway, no, I never lose interest in watching. My cousin and I actually watch the evening games together, though he always complains that I have the volume up too loud. 

And my projects? Heavens no, I still love my projects. I love tinkering out in the garage. Just last week I was out there working on my workbench. I have this whole pegboard system for my hand tools that I've been meaning to optimize. Well, I *started* optimizing it, anyway. I got all the screwdrivers lined up perfectly by size—Phillips head, flathead, your square drives, the whole lot—and the desire to do it, the enjoyment I get out of just working with my hands? That's all very much still there. I don't get down in the dumps or just want to lay in bed all day, if that's what you're getting at. 

My mood is generally quite good, really. I still very much enjoy my hobbies and my days. It's just... well, like I was saying before, I might get halfway through hanging those tools and then get completely sidetracked trying to find the exact right size metal hook for my rubber mallet, and then I'll end up leaving half the wrenches sitting out on the bench overnight. Or I'll be watching the game and completely forget where I set my glasses down during the seventh-inning stretch. But the enthusiasm? The actual drive to do the things I enjoy? No, that hasn't changed a bit.
Do these attention and focus problems happen in different places, like at home, at church, or when you're out running errands, or do they mostly occur in just one setting?

Well, different places... you know, I honestly couldn't tell you if there's a pattern to it like that. I really haven't stopped to think about whether it's strictly a home thing or an everywhere thing. Because, well, my days are fairly varied, even though I haven't been in the workforce for a bit. Like I mentioned, I'm at home a lot with my cousin's recovery, which is its own little ecosystem of activity, what with the home health nurse and the physical therapist coming by. Her name is Brenda, by the way, the therapist—lovely woman, very firm about his leg lifts, which he complains about constantly, but she gets results. 

But then, of course, I'm also over at the church, or I'm out running errands. And speaking of errands, if you want to talk about losing track of things, the grocery store we go to over on Route 9 just completely rearranged their entire layout last month. It's a disaster. You go in looking for crushed tomatoes, which have been in aisle four since we moved here, and suddenly they're all the way over in aisle twelve next to the baking supplies! It makes absolutely no logical sense. So if I'm standing there in the middle of the store looking completely lost, is it because my focus drifted off again, or is it just because the store manager decided to play a practical joke on the shoppers? It's hard to say! 

So, to answer your question, I really don't know. I haven't kept a careful enough tally to say if it's mostly occurring in just one setting or if it follows me around everywhere I go. I just sort of go about my day and deal with the wandering mind whenever it happens to pop up, without really noting down exactly where I am at the time.
Have you noticed any days when you feel unusually tired or lacking in energy, even if you’ve had a good night’s sleep?

Unusually tired? Lacking energy? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I really wouldn't. My energy levels are just fine, I think. I mean, I'm fifty-nine, so I'm not exactly going to be out there running marathons or, you know, doing backflips in the yard, but I certainly don't have days where I'm just dragging my feet for no reason. 

Now, sleep, that's a whole other topic, isn't it? My wife, she swears by this chamomile tea before bed. She gets the loose-leaf kind from that little natural foods store downtown—the one with the creaky wooden floors that always smells faintly of patchouli and dried apples. She brews a pot every single night around nine-thirty, and she says it knocks her right out. I've tried it a few times, but honestly, it just makes me have to get up to use the restroom at two in the morning, which completely defeats the purpose of a good night's sleep if you ask me! 

But even with the occasional midnight trip to the bathroom, I wake up feeling perfectly fine. I'm up with the sun, usually. I like to get out to the kitchen and get the coffee going before my cousin starts stirring, because once he's up, it's a whole production with getting his walker positioned and making sure he's taken his morning anti-inflammatories. So I need my energy to be ready for that, and thankfully, it is. I don't feel unusually fatigued or drained. If I'm physically tired, it's usually because I actually *did* something tiring, like spending three hours trying to weed the flowerbeds out front. The dandelions this year, I tell you, they are absolutely relentless. You pull one, and three more pop up in its place by the next morning! It's like fighting a hydra out there. But no, no mysterious lack of energy or anything like that. I feel perfectly normal in that department.
Have you ever found yourself staring at a task, knowing you need to start it, but feeling mentally stuck or unable to get going—even when it's something simple or routine?

Staring at a task? Mentally stuck? No, I really don't think I've ever experienced anything quite like that. I'm actually quite the self-starter, to be perfectly honest with you. When I see something that needs doing, I don't just stand there paralyzed, I just dive right in. 

Take the daily mail, for example. Our mail carrier—Frank, nice guy, though for the life of me I don't understand why he insists on wearing his uniform shorts well into November when there's a chill in the air—he drops the mail through the slot usually right around eleven-thirty. I don't just sit there staring at the pile on the entryway table feeling unable to deal with it. Heavens, no. I walk right over, and I grab my letter opener. I have this wonderful heavy brass one I picked up at a gift shop in Washington D.C. back in '98, shaped like an eagle feather. Beautiful piece of craftsmanship, really. Anyway, I take that opener and I slice right into the envelopes immediately. The electric bill, the glossy flyers for that new pizza place over on 4th street, the endless, absolutely endless stream of credit card offers... I start sorting them right then and there. 

So, no, I don't get that mentally stuck feeling you're describing. I don't look at the vacuum cleaner or the lawnmower and think, "Oh, I just can't bring myself to turn it on." If the rug needs vacuuming, I pull the Hoover out of the hall closet, plug it in, and get right to it. Now, whether I actually finish vacuuming the entire living room before I notice a scuff mark on the baseboard and wander off to the kitchen to find a sponge and some soapy water... well, that's a different story, like we were talking about earlier with my tools. But the actual starting part? The getting going? No, I've never had an issue with that. I just jump right in without a second thought.
Do you feel like these attention and memory problems are significantly interfering with your ability to manage your daily responsibilities, even with your systems in place?

Well, see, that’s the rub, isn't it? I try to have my little systems, but... honestly, yes, it is starting to get in the way. It’s actually causing quite a bit of tension at home lately, which I hate to admit. My wife—she’s a very patient woman, usually, but even she has her limits, and she’s told me flat out recently that she feels like she just can’t count on me when it comes to my cousin’s care. And that hurts to hear, it really does, because I am trying. 

But, for instance, the other day I was supposed to make sure he did his afternoon leg extensions—the ones Brenda the physical therapist was so firm about—before his ice pack went on. And I fully intended to! But on my way to get the ice pack, I noticed the hinge on the pantry door was a little loose, so I went to find my screwdriver, and... well, I got completely sidetracked, and the exercises just never happened. My wife came home, saw the ice pack still sitting in the freezer, and let's just say it was a very quiet dinner that night. She feels like she has to manage *me* on top of managing his recovery, which just isn't fair to her, and it's putting a real strain on things.

And it’s spilling over into my other responsibilities, too. I know I’m not working a regular nine-to-five anymore, but I do take on these little catering tasks—mostly for the church and a few local community center events. You know, organizing the food, setting up the trays, making sure everything is where it needs to be. It used to be a breeze, but lately, I’ve had to constantly double-check absolutely everything I do, or even completely redo things, just so the small jobs don’t get mixed up. 

Just last week, for example, I was doing a small luncheon setup for the rotary club, and I completely lost track of which sandwiches had the horseradish mayo and which were plain. I was supposed to put little frilly toothpicks in the horseradish ones, but my mind had drifted off to thinking about whether we had enough folding chairs in the storage closet, and I just kept making sandwiches without marking them. I ended up having to unwrap and check almost three dozen sandwiches, one by one, and basically redo the entire platter because I was terrified I'd give horseradish to someone with a sensitive stomach! So, yes, to answer your question, even with me trying my hardest to keep things organized, it’s definitely interfering. It takes me twice as long to get things done because I’m always having to backtrack.
Have you ever found yourself acting without thinking things through, like interrupting others, blurting out answers, or feeling restless and unable to sit still for long?

Interrupting others? Blurting things out? Oh, goodness, no. That’s really not my personality at all. If anything, I’m the exact opposite in those situations. 

You know, my wife’s sister, Diane, now *she* is an interrupter. You can barely get a word in edgewise at Thanksgiving when she comes to visit. She’ll ask you a question, like how the mashed potatoes turned out, and before you can even get out the word "good," she’s already off on a tangent about some recipe she saw on the Food Network that uses truffle oil and chives. It's exhausting, frankly. But me? I just sit back and let people talk. My mother always taught me it’s polite to wait your turn, so I really make an effort to just listen. Now, whether I actually absorb everything they're saying or if my mind wanders off to something else entirely... well, that happens, sure. But I certainly don't cut people off or blurt things out before they're finished speaking. I'm much more of a ponderer. 

And as for feeling restless or not being able to sit still... no, I don't have that problem at all. I can sit perfectly fine for long stretches. Take Sunday mornings, for instance. Pastor Dave—he’s a wonderful man, very dedicated to the congregation, but his sermons can really stretch on. Just last week he was going on and on about the Book of Daniel for a solid forty-five minutes. I could see people in the pews shifting around, checking their watches, letting out these heavy little sighs, but I was just sitting there, perfectly content to stay put. 

Same thing at home. I have this old dark green La-Z-Boy recliner in the den. I bought it back in... oh, it must have been 2010, right after they remodeled that big furniture showroom out on Route 9. I can sit in that chair for hours, just drinking my coffee and looking out the window at the bird feeder. We get these absolutely beautiful cardinals this time of year, and the blue jays have been very active lately, too. So, no, sitting still is quite easy for me. I don't get that antsy, jump-out-of-my-skin feeling you're talking about. I'm much more likely to be sitting perfectly still, just lost in my own thoughts, rather than bouncing off the walls or acting without thinking.

Have you noticed any decline in your ability to plan or organize your daily activities, such as difficulty following a plan you've made or trouble thinking through the steps needed to complete a task?

Decline in planning? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. If anything, the planning part is something I'm still quite excellent at. I don't have any trouble whatsoever figuring out the steps to get something done or making a schedule. 

Take the church pancake breakfast, for instance. We do it the first Saturday of every month, and I’m the one who organizes the whole kitchen operation. I sit down at the dining room table the Wednesday before with my yellow legal pad—I always use those legal pads with the narrow blue lines, I just can't stand the wide-ruled ones, they make my handwriting look absolutely enormous—and I map out the entire morning. I calculate exactly how many bags of flour we need, the gallons of buttermilk, the logistics of who is on the griddle and who is taking tickets at the door. I can see all the steps perfectly in my head, right down to the minute. Step one, get the coffee urns plugged in by six-fifteen because they take a solid forty minutes to brew. Step two, mix the dry ingredients. Step three, get the sausage links in the oven. I know exactly how to get from point A to point B, and I don't sit there confused about what the next step should be. 

Same thing with my cousin's care. I have his whole medication and physical therapy schedule written out on this big whiteboard on the fridge. I color-coded it and everything—blue for the pills, red for the exercises, green for doctor's appointments. So the actual ability to make a plan and think through exactly what needs to happen? The blueprint is always right there in my head, clear as a bell. I haven't noticed any decline there at all. 

Now, like I was saying earlier, whether I can actually *execute* that plan without getting distracted by a loose hinge on the pantry door on my way to fetch an ice pack... well, that's where things go a little sideways. But the planning itself? The organizing of the steps? No, I'm perfectly fine in that department. I'm still the one everyone calls when they need a timeline sorted out for the community center events.

Looking back on your childhood and younger years, did you have similar issues with forgetfulness, distraction, or not finishing tasks, or is this something that only started more recently as an adult?

Childhood? Oh, well... yes, actually. It really isn't just a recent thing at all. I mean, if I really think back on it, to when I was just a little boy in grade school, definitely well before I was twelve years old, it was the exact same story. 

I remember it so clearly. I went to Lincoln Elementary, which was one of those beautiful old brick buildings with the massive oak front doors that took your whole body weight to pull open. Anyway, my mother, God rest her soul, she would come home from those parent-teacher conferences in the fall and sit me down at our yellow Formica kitchen table. And she would always have this heavy sigh, because every single year, whether it was Mrs. Higgins in third grade or Mr. Abernathy in fifth, the teachers told my parents the exact same thing. They always said I was a very bright boy, which I suppose was their polite way of softening the blow, but they said I was just constantly daydreaming. 

And they weren't wrong, honestly! I would be staring out the classroom window, watching the school custodian rake the leaves or just completely lost in my own little world, thinking about a book I was reading or a bug I found on the sidewalk, instead of looking at the chalkboard. 

And my desk... oh, my goodness. You remember those old wooden desks where the whole top lifts up on a hinge? Mine was an absolute disaster area. I would actually do my homework at home, sitting right at that yellow kitchen table, but then I'd just shove it in there and leave my homework in my desk instead of walking it up to the teacher's turn-in tray. It was just a graveyard of crumpled math worksheets and spelling tests in there. And during the actual school day, they constantly had to give me reminders just to finish my classwork. I'd get halfway through a page of long division and then just... drift away. The teachers were always having to walk down the aisle and tap on my desk to tell me to come back to earth and finish my assignment. So, yes, to answer your question, this forgetfulness and drifting off has been going on for a very, very long time.
When you think back to your school years, were these issues with attention and finishing tasks something you noticed in yourself consistently throughout childhood, or did they come and go?

Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, it really was a constant thing. It didn't just come and go like a passing phase or a bad week here and there, no. Even back in grade school, well before I turned twelve, it was the exact same story every single year. 

Like I mentioned, my parents would go to those conferences—they used to set them up in the school gymnasium, all the teachers sitting at these little brown folding tables with the squeaky metal chairs—and every time, without fail, the teachers told my parents the same thing. They’d say, "He’s a very bright boy, but he is always daydreaming." It didn't matter if it was September or May, third grade or sixth grade, I was consistently off in my own world. 

And the homework situation... well, I know I already told you about that absolute mess in my desk, but that wasn't just a once-in-a-while mistake! That was an everyday occurrence. I was always leaving my finished homework shoved in there instead of actually handing it in to the teacher. And they were constantly—I mean, every single day—having to give me reminders to finish my classwork. It was just... my normal. Well, see, that’s the rub, isn't it? I try to have my little systems, but... honestly, yes, it is starting to get in the way. My wife came home, saw the ice pack still sitting in the freezer, and let's just say it was a very quiet dinner that night. She feels like she has to manage *me* on top of managing his recovery, which just isn't fair to her, and it's putting a real strain on things.

And it’s spilling over into my other responsibilities, too. I know I’m not working a regular nine-to-five anymore, but I do take on these little catering tasks—mostly for the church and a few local community center events. You know, organizing the food, setting up the trays, making sure everything is where it needs to be. It used to be a breeze, but lately, I’ve had to constantly double-check absolutely everything I do, or even completely redo things, just so the small jobs don’t get mixed up. 

Just last week, for example, I was doing a small luncheon setup for the rotary club, and I completely lost track of which sandwiches had the horseradish mayo and which were plain. I was supposed to put little frilly toothpicks in the horseradish ones, but my mind had drifted off to thinking about whether we had enough folding chairs in the storage closet, and I just kept making sandwiches without marking them. I ended up having to unwrap and check almost three dozen sandwiches, one by one, and basically redo the entire platter because I was terrified I'd give horseradish to someone with a sensitive stomach! So, yes, to answer your question, even with me trying my hardest to keep things organized, it’s definitely interfering. It takes me twice as long to get things done because I’m always having to backtrack.

Now, whether I actually absorb everything they're saying or if my mind wanders off to something else entirely... well, that happens, sure. But I certainly don't cut people off or blurt things out before they're finished speaking. I'm much more of a ponderer. 

And as for feeling restless or not being able to sit still... no, I don't have that problem at all. I can sit perfectly fine for long stretches. Take Sunday mornings, for instance. Pastor Dave—he’s a wonderful man, very dedicated to the congregation, but his sermons can really stretch on. Just last week he was going on and on about the Book of Daniel for a solid forty-five minutes. I could see people in the pews shifting around, checking their watches, letting out these heavy little sighs, but I was just sitting there, perfectly content to stay put. 

Same thing at home. I have this old dark green La-Z-Boy recliner in the den. I bought it back in... oh, it must have been 2010, right after they remodeled that big furniture showroom out on Route 9. I can sit in that chair for hours, just drinking my coffee and looking out the window at the bird feeder. We get these absolutely beautiful cardinals this time of year, and the blue jays have been very active lately, too. So, no, sitting still is quite easy for me. I don't get that antsy, jump-out-of-my-skin feeling you're talking about. I calculate exactly how many bags of flour we need, the gallons of buttermilk, the logistics of who is on the griddle and who is taking tickets at the door. I can see all the steps perfectly in my head, right down to the minute. Step one, get the coffee urns plugged in by six-fifteen because they take a solid forty minutes to brew. I color-coded it and everything—blue for the pills, red for the exercises, green for doctor's appointments. So the actual ability to make a plan and think through exactly what needs to happen? The blueprint is always right there in my head, clear as a bell. I haven't noticed any decline there at all. 

Now, like I was saying earlier, whether I can actually *execute* that plan without getting distracted by a loose hinge on the pantry door on my way to fetch an ice pack... well, that's where things go a little sideways. And she would always have this heavy sigh, because every single year, whether it was Mrs. Higgins in third grade or Mr. Abernathy in fifth, the teachers told my parents the exact same thing. And my desk... oh, my goodness. You remember those old wooden desks where the whole top lifts up on a hinge? Mine was an absolute disaster area. It was just a graveyard of crumpled math worksheets and spelling tests in there. And during the actual school day, they constantly had to give me reminders just to finish my classwork. I'd get halfway through a page of long division and then just... drift away. The teachers were always having to walk down the aisle and tap on my desk to tell me to come back to earth and finish my assignment.
